}

  2. Open workspace in your IDE

  3. Both repos are accessible

docs.title: For Testing Plugins
docs.text:
When developing plugins, you can:

  1. Test locally by installing from the local path: 

    # In calvin-plugins/weather-plugin
# Copy to calvin's plugin directory for testing
cp -r weather-plugin /path/to/calvin/backend/data/plugins/weather

  2. Use the plugin installer's repo support:

  3. Point to local path: file:///path/to/calvin-plugins

  4. Or use the GitHub URL for testing

  5. Development workflow:

  6. Edit plugin in calvin-plugins repo
  7. Test by installing from local path or GitHub
  8. Commit and push when ready

docs.title: 1. Configure Python Paths
docs.text:
In workspace settings, ensure Python can find both repos:

{
  "python.analysis.extraPaths": [
    "${workspaceFolder:Calvin}/backend",
    "${workspaceFolder:Calvin Plugins}"
  ]
}

docs.title: 2. Use Multi-Root Search
docs.text:
• Ctrl+Shift+F (Windows) or Cmd+Shift+F (Mac) searches across all workspace folders
  • Use files to include filter to search specific repos

docs.title: 3. Configure Git
docs.text: If using multi-root workspace, your IDE handles Git for each folder separately. You can: - Commit to each repo independently - See separate Git status in source control panel

docs.title: 4. Extension Settings
docs.text: Extensions work across all workspace folders. Configure once, applies to both.

docs.title: Repository Organization
docs.text:
1. Keep plugins independent: Each plugin should work standalone
  2. Version plugins: Use semantic versioning in plugin.json
  3. Document plugins: Include README in each plugin directory
  4. Test before submitting: Ensure plugins work with latest Calvin version

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
1. Develop in calvin-plugins: Create/edit plugins there
  2. Test in calvin: Install and test plugins in main repo
  3. Version control: Commit to appropriate repo
  4. Release: Tag releases in plugins repo

docs.title: CI/CD Considerations
docs.text:
• Plugins repo: Can have its own CI for plugin validation
  • Main repo: Tests core functionality, may test against plugin repo
  • Integration: Can set up workflows to test plugins against main repo

cd my-new-plugin

  2. Test locally:

  3. Update plugins.json:

  4. Commit and push:

git commit -m "Add my-new-plugin"
git push

  5. Users install:

  6. Enter https://github.com/your-org/calvin-plugins in Settings
  7. Browse and install my-new-plugin

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ✅ Create calvin-plugins repository for better organization
  • ✅ Use multi-root workspace for best development experience
  • ✅ Keep plugins independent and well-documented
  • ✅ Test locally before publishing
  • ✅ Version control separately but coordinate releases

This setup gives you the flexibility to develop plugins independently while maintaining a clean separation between core and plugins.

docs.title: CI/CD for Docker Images
docs.text: Calvin Dashboard uses GitHub Actions to automatically build and push Docker images to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The CI/CD pipeline automatically: - Builds multi-architecture Docker images (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) - Pushes images to ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend and ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-frontend - Tags images appropriately based on branch or tag - Uses build caching for faster builds

docs.title: Workflow Triggers
docs.text: The workflow runs on: - Push to main branch: Builds and pushes images tagged with main and latest - Push to develop branch: Builds and pushes images tagged with develop - Git tags (e.g., v1.0.0): Builds and pushes versioned images - Pull requests: Builds images but doesn't push (for testing) - Manual trigger: Can be manually triggered from GitHub Actions UI

docs.title: Image Tags
docs.text: Images are automatically tagged with: - Branch name: main, develop (for branch pushes) - Version tags: v1.0.0, 1.0.0, 1.0 (for git tags) - Latest: latest (only for main branch)

docs.title: Example Tags
docs.text:
For a push to main: - ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:main - ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:latest

For a git tag v1.2.3: - ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:v1.2.3 - ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:1.2.3 - ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:1.2

docs.title: Pulling Images
docs.text:
# Pull latest images
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:latest
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-frontend:latest

# Pull specific version
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:v1.0.0
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-frontend:v1.0.0

# Pull from develop branch
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:develop
docker pull ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-frontend:develop

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
To pull images from GHCR, you may need to authenticate:

# Using GitHub Personal Access Token
echo $GITHUB_TOKEN | docker login ghcr.io -u USERNAME --password-stdin

# Or using GitHub CLI
gh auth token | docker login ghcr.io -u USERNAME --password-stdin

docs.title: Using in Docker Compose
docs.text:
Update your docker-compose.yml to use pre-built images:

services:
  calvin-backend:
    image: ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-backend:latest
    # ... rest of config

  calvin-frontend:
    image: ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin-frontend:latest
    # ... rest of config

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text:
For local development, you can still build images manually:

# Build locally
cd docker
docker build -f Dockerfile.backend-prod -t calvin-backend:local ..
docker build -f Dockerfile.frontend-prod -t calvin-frontend:local ..

Or use docker-compose:

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml build

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Support
docs.text:
All images are built for: - linux/amd64 - Intel/AMD 64-bit - linux/arm64 - ARM 64-bit (Apple Silicon, modern Raspberry Pi) - linux/arm/v7 - ARM 32-bit (Raspberry Pi 3B+ and older)

Docker will automatically select the correct architecture for your platform.

docs.title: Build Caching
docs.text: The CI/CD pipeline uses GitHub Actions cache to speed up builds: - Build layers are cached between runs - Only changed layers are rebuilt - Significantly reduces build time

docs.title: Manual Workflow Trigger
docs.text:
You can manually trigger the workflow from GitHub:

  1. Go to Actions tab in GitHub
  2. Select Build and Push Docker Images
  3. Click Run workflow
  4. Optionally enable Push images to registry
  5. Click Run workflow

docs.title: Monitoring Builds
docs.text:
• View build status in the Actions tab
  • Check build logs for any issues
  • Images are automatically published to GHCR on successful builds

docs.title: Build Failures
docs.text: If builds fail: 1. Check the Actions logs for error messages 2. Verify Dockerfile syntax 3. Check for dependency issues 4. Ensure all required files are present

docs.title: Authentication Issues
docs.text: If you can't pull images: 1. Ensure you're authenticated with GHCR 2. Check that the repository is public or you have access 3. Verify your GitHub token has read:packages permission

docs.title: Architecture-Specific Issues
docs.text: If an image doesn't work on your platform: 1. Verify the architecture is supported (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) 2. Check that Docker is correctly detecting your platform 3. Try pulling a specific architecture: docker pull --platform linux/amd64 ghcr.io/...

docs.title: Building and Running Docker Containers
docs.text: This guide covers how to build and run Calvin Dashboard using Docker containers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine 20.10+ or Docker Desktop
  • Docker Compose 2.0+ (usually included with Docker Desktop)
  • For multi-architecture builds: Docker Buildx (usually included with Docker)

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
# Start development containers with hot-reload
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up

# Or run in background
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up -d

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml down

docs.title: Production (Local - Monolithic)
docs.text:
# Build and start
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d calvin-prod

docs.text:
Backend Server: 

export CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

Frontend (Raspberry Pi): 

export BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

docs.title: Backend Only
docs.text:
cd docker
docker build -f Dockerfile.backend-prod -t calvin-backend:latest ..

docs.title: Frontend Only
docs.text:
cd docker
docker build -f Dockerfile.frontend-prod -t calvin-frontend:latest \
  --build-arg VITE_API_URL=/api ..

docs.title: Development Backend
docs.text:
cd docker
docker build -f Dockerfile.backend-dev -t calvin-backend-dev:latest \
  ..

docs.title: Development Frontend
docs.text:
cd docker
docker build -f Dockerfile.frontend-dev -t calvin-frontend-dev:latest \

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Builds
docs.text: For building images that support multiple architectures (amd64, arm64, arm/v7):

docs.title: Using the Build Script
docs.text:
cd docker

# Build for all architectures and push to registry
./build-multiarch.sh --both --push --repo your-registry/calvin --tag latest

# Build only backend
./build-multiarch.sh --backend --push --repo your-registry/calvin

# Build only frontend
./build-multiarch.sh --frontend --push --repo your-registry/calvin

# Build for specific architectures
./build-multiarch.sh --both --push --repo your-registry/calvin \
  --arch linux/amd64,linux/arm64

# Build for local use (single platform only)
./build-multiarch.sh --both --arch linux/amd64

Note: Multi-platform builds require pushing to a registry. For local builds, specify a single platform.

docs.title: Using Docker Buildx Directly
docs.text:
# Create buildx builder (first time only)
docker buildx create --name calvin-multiarch --use
docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

# Build and push backend
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  --file docker/Dockerfile.backend-prod \
  --tag your-registry/calvin-backend:latest \
  --push \
  .

# Build and push frontend
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  --file docker/Dockerfile.frontend-prod \
  --build-arg VITE_API_URL=/api \
  --tag your-registry/calvin-frontend:latest \
  --push \
  .

docs.title: Using Pre-built Images from Registry
docs.text:
If images are available in a registry:

# Pull images
docker pull your-registry/calvin-backend:latest
docker pull your-registry/calvin-frontend:latest

# Tag for local use
docker tag your-registry/calvin-backend:latest calvin-backend:latest
docker tag your-registry/calvin-frontend:latest calvin-frontend:latest

# Use with docker-compose
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod-separate.yml up -d

docs.title: Development Mode
docs.text:
Development mode uses hot-reload for both backend and frontend:

# Start development containers
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up

# Access:
# - Backend API: http://localhost:8000
# - Frontend Dev Server: http://localhost:5173
# - API Docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

Features: - Code changes trigger automatic reload - Source code mounted as volumes - Fast iteration cycle - Separate ports for backend (8000) and frontend (5173)

docs.title: Production Mode (Separate Containers)
docs.text:
Production mode uses optimized images with separate containers:

# Start production containers
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod-separate.yml up -d

# Access:
# - Backend API: http://localhost:8000
# - Frontend: http://localhost:80
# - API Docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

Features: - Optimized multi-stage builds - Nginx for frontend static file serving - Separate containers for scalability - Production-ready configuration

docs.title: Production Mode (Monolithic)
docs.text:
Legacy single-container deployment:

# Start monolithic container
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d calvin-prod

# Access:
# - Application: http://localhost:8000
# - API Docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

Features: - Single container for simplicity - Backend serves frontend static files - All-in-one deployment - Backwards compatible

docs.title: Distributed Deployment
docs.text: Run backend and frontend on separate machines:

docs.title: Step 1: Backend Server
docs.text:
On the machine hosting the backend (e.g., home server):

# Set CORS origins (comma-separated)
export CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80,http://rpi.local:80

# Start backend
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

# Backend available at: http://backend-ip:8000

docs.title: Step 2: Frontend
docs.text:
On the machine hosting the frontend (e.g., Raspberry Pi):

# Set backend URL
export BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api

# Start frontend
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

# Frontend available at: http://localhost:80

Important Notes: - Backend URL is embedded at build time, so you must rebuild the frontend image if the backend URL changes - Ensure CORS is properly configured on the backend - Verify network connectivity between machines - Consider firewall rules

docs.title: Using VS Code Dev Containers
docs.text: VS Code dev containers provide a fully configured development environment:

docs.title: Prerequisites

• VS Code with Dev Containers extension

docs.title: Opening in Dev Container

1. Open VS Code in the project root
  2. Press F1 or Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows/Linux) / Cmd+Shift+P (Mac)

docs.title: Customization

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml stop

# Stop and remove containers (keeps volumes)
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml down

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml build

# Rebuild specific service
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml build calvin-backend-dev

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml build --no-cache

# Rebuild and restart
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up -d --build

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
Calvin Dashboard uses Docker volumes for data persistence:

  • calvin-data - Database, images, and configuration
  • calvin-logs - Application logs
  • backend-venv (dev) - Python virtual environment
  • frontend-node-modules (dev) - Node.js modules

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
# Backup data volume
docker run --rm -v calvin-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/calvin-data-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

# Backup logs
docker run --rm -v calvin-logs:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/calvin-logs-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

docs.text:
# Restore data volume
docker run --rm -v calvin-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine sh -c "cd /data && tar xzf /backup/calvin-data-backup.tar.gz"

# Restore logs
docker run --rm -v calvin-logs:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine sh -c "cd /data && tar xzf /backup/calvin-logs-backup.tar.gz"

docs.title: Port Already in Use

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml logs

# Linux

sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp

  env | grep CORS

docs.title: Docker Overview
docs.text:
This document provides an overview of Docker deployment options for Calvin Dashboard.

Note: For detailed getting started instructions, see Getting Started with Docker. For detailed build and run instructions, see Docker Building and Running.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Calvin Dashboard can be deployed in several ways: 1. Monolithic - Backend and frontend in a single container (legacy) 2. Separate Containers - Backend and frontend in separate containers on the same machine 3. Distributed - Backend on one machine (e.g., home server) and frontend on another (e.g., Raspberry Pi)

All Dockerfiles support multi-architecture builds (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) for deployment on various platforms including Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: Local Deployment (Separate Containers)
docs.text:
Deploy both backend and frontend on the same machine:

# From project root
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod-separate.yml up -d

# Backend: http://localhost:8000
# Frontend: http://localhost:80

docs.title: Step 1: Backend Server (e.g., Home Server)
docs.text:
On the machine hosting the backend:

# Set CORS origins to allow your frontend machine(s)
export CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80,http://rpi.local:80

# Start backend only
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

# Backend will be available at http://backend-server:8000

docs.title: Step 2: Frontend (e.g., Raspberry Pi)
docs.text:
On the machine hosting the frontend:

# Set the backend URL
export BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api

# Start frontend only
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

# Frontend will be available at http://localhost:80

docs.title: Legacy Monolithic Deployment
docs.text:
For backwards compatibility, the monolithic container is still available:

# From project root
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d calvin-prod

# Access at http://localhost:8000

docs.title: Development with Hot-Reload
docs.text:
# From project root
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up

# Backend: http://localhost:8000 (auto-reloads on code changes)
# Frontend: http://localhost:5173 (Vite dev server with HMR)

docs.title: VS Code Dev Containers
docs.text:
For a fully configured development environment in VS Code:

  1. Install the Dev Containers extension
  2. Open the project in VS Code
  3. Press F1 and select "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container"
  4. VS Code will build and start the containers automatically

Note: If you don't have a .devcontainer directory yet, you can create one based on the Docker development setup. See the Getting Started with Docker guide for details.

docs.title: 1. Backend (Dockerfile.backend-prod)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Production backend API server
  • Features:
  • Multi-stage build (optimized size)
  • Python 3.11 with UV
  • FastAPI/uvicorn
  • Port: 8000
  • Use case: Backend API server

docs.title: 2. Frontend (Dockerfile.frontend-prod)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Production frontend web server
  • Features:
  • Multi-stage build (optimized size)
  • Nginx for static file serving
  • Built Vue.js application
  • Port: 80
  • Use case: Frontend web interface

docs.title: 3. Monolithic (Dockerfile.prod)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Legacy single-container deployment
  • Features:
  • Both backend and frontend in one container
  • Backend serves frontend static files
  • Port: 8000
  • Use case: Simple single-machine deployment

docs.title: 1. Development with Hot-Reload (docker-compose.dev.yml)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Active development
  • Features:
  • Mounts local code as volumes
  • Hot-reload on code changes
  • Separate backend/frontend containers
  • Use case: Local development, rapid testing

docs.title: 2. Development Image (Dockerfile.dev-prod)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Development/testing on Raspberry Pi
  • Features:
  • Auto-pulls latest code from GitHub
  • Auto-updates dependencies
  • Auto-rebuilds frontend
  • Auto-restarts services
  • Use case: Testing on RPi without reflashing

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Builds
docs.text:
To build images for multiple architectures (amd64, arm64, arm/v7):

Note: Multi-architecture builds require pushing to a registry. The --load option only works with single-platform builds.

# Build and push to registry (for multi-architecture)
cd docker
./build-multiarch.sh --both --push --repo your-registry/calvin --tag latest

# Build only backend for specific architectures
./build-multiarch.sh --backend --push --repo your-registry/calvin --arch linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7

# Build with custom API URL for frontend
VITE_API_URL=http://backend:8000/api ./build-multiarch.sh --frontend --push --repo your-registry/calvin

# Build for local use (single platform, current architecture)
./build-multiarch.sh --both  # Builds for current platform only

docs.title: Prerequisites for Multi-Architecture Builds
docs.text:
1. Docker with buildx support
  2. QEMU for cross-platform emulation (usually installed automatically)

The script will create a buildx builder if it doesn't exist.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
• DATABASE_URL - Database connection string (default: sqlite:///app/data/db/calvin.db)
  • IMAGE_DIR - Image storage directory (default: /app/data/images)
  • CORS_ORIGINS - Comma-separated list of allowed CORS origins (required for distributed deployment)
  • CORS_ALLOW_ALL - Allow all origins (development only, default: false)

docs.title: Distributed Deployment
docs.text:
When running backend separately, you must configure CORS:

# Example: Allow frontend on Raspberry Pi
export CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80,http://rpi.local:80

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

Or edit the docker-compose file:

environment:
  - CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80,http://rpi.local:80

docs.title: Build Arguments
docs.text:
• VITE_API_URL - Backend API URL (set at build time)
  • For local deployment: /api (relative URL)
  • For distributed deployment: http://backend-host:8000/api (absolute URL)

docs.title: Distributed Deployment
docs.text:
When running frontend separately, you must set the backend URL:

# Example: Backend at 192.168.1.100:8000
export BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

Or edit the docker-compose file:

build:
  args:
    - VITE_API_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api

Note: The API URL is embedded at build time. To change it, rebuild the image.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Local Development
docs.text:
Both backend and frontend on your development machine:

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.dev.yml up

docs.title: Scenario 2: Single Machine Production
docs.text:
Backend and frontend on the same machine:

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.prod-separate.yml up -d

docs.title: Scenario 3: Distributed Production
docs.text:
Backend on home server, frontend on Raspberry Pi:

On Home Server: 

# Configure CORS for frontend machine
export CORS_ORIGINS=http://192.168.1.50:80

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

On Raspberry Pi: 

# Configure backend URL
export BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000/api

docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

docs.title: Scenario 4: Multiple Frontends
docs.text:
Run one backend server and multiple frontend instances:

Backend Server: 

export CORS_ORIGINS=http://rpi1.local:80,http://rpi2.local:80,http://rpi3.local:80
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.backend-only.yml up -d

Each Frontend (different machines): 

export BACKEND_URL=http://backend-server:8000/api
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.frontend-only.yml up -d

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
The following volumes are used:

  • calvin-data - Persistent data storage (database, images, etc.)
  • calvin-logs - Application logs

Data persists across container restarts and updates.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
All containers use the calvin-network bridge network for local communication.

For distributed deployment, containers communicate over the host network (default Docker networking).

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
Both backend and frontend containers include health checks:

  • Backend: Checks /api/health endpoint
  • Frontend: Checks /health endpoint (nginx)

Health check status can be viewed with:

docker ps
# Check STATUS column for (healthy) or (unhealthy)

docs.title: CORS Errors in Distributed Deployment
docs.text:
If you see CORS errors when frontend tries to connect to backend:

  1. Verify CORS_ORIGINS includes the frontend URL
  2. Check that the frontend URL matches exactly (including protocol and port)
  3. Ensure backend is accessible from frontend machine (firewall, network)

docs.title: Frontend Cannot Connect to Backend
docs.text:
1. Verify BACKEND_URL is correct and accessible
  2. Test backend connectivity: curl http://backend-host:8000/api/health
  3. Check firewall rules on backend machine
  4. Verify network connectivity between machines

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Build Issues
docs.text:
If buildx fails:

  1. Ensure Docker has buildx support: docker buildx version
  2. Create builder manually: docker buildx create --name calvin-multiarch --use
  3. Bootstrap builder: docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

docs.title: Advantages of Docker Approach
docs.text:
1. Isolation: Clean environment, no conflicts
  2. Portability: Same image works everywhere
  3. Multi-Architecture: Support for amd64, arm64, arm/v7
  4. Flexibility: Separate or combined deployments
  5. Easy Updates: Just pull new image
  6. Rollback: Easy to revert to previous image
  7. Development: Hot-reload without affecting system
  8. Dev Containers: Fully configured VS Code development environment

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
1. Overhead: Slight performance overhead
  2. Complexity: Additional layer of abstraction
  3. Storage: Images take up space

For Raspberry Pi 3B+, Docker overhead is minimal and the benefits outweigh the costs.

docs.title: Getting Started with Calvin
docs.text: Welcome to Calvin! This guide will help you get started with Calvin Dashboard, whether you're setting up for development or production deployment.

docs.title: Choose Your Setup Method
docs.text:
Calvin supports multiple setup methods depending on your needs:

  1. Native Installation - Direct installation on your system (recommended for development)
  2. Windows: Automated PowerShell script
  3. Linux/Raspberry Pi: Automated bash scripts

  4. Manual Setup: Step-by-step manual installation

  5. Docker Setup - Containerized deployment (recommended for production and consistent environments)

  6. Development with hot-reload
  7. Production deployment

  8. Distributed deployment (backend and frontend on separate machines)

  9. VS Code Dev Containers - Fully configured development environment in containers

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin, ensure you have:

  • Python 3.11+ - Download Python
  • Node.js 20+ (LTS recommended) - Download Node.js
  • Git - Download Git
  • UV - Python package manager (installed automatically by setup scripts)

docs.title: Platform-Specific Notes
docs.text:
• Windows: Keyboard input uses a mock handler (normal for development). Full keyboard support works on Linux/Raspberry Pi.
  • Linux/Raspberry Pi: Full keyboard support available via evdev package.
  • Docker: Works on all platforms that support Docker.

docs.title: Windows Development Setup
docs.text: The easiest way to get started on Windows is using the automated setup script.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin

# 2. Run the setup script
.\setup-windows.ps1

# 3. Start development servers
.\make.ps1 dev

The setup script will: - Check for Python 3.11+, Node.js 20+, and Git - Install UV if not present - Switch to the develop branch (if Git is available) - Install all backend dependencies (with dev extras) - Install all frontend dependencies

docs.title: Manual Setup
docs.text:
If you prefer manual setup or the script doesn't work for your environment:

# Install backend dependencies
cd backend
uv sync --extra dev
cd ..

# Install frontend dependencies
cd frontend
npm install
cd ..

# Start development servers (in separate terminals)
# Terminal 1 - Backend:
cd backend
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

# Terminal 2 - Frontend:
cd frontend
npm run dev

Access Points: - Backend API: http://localhost:8000 - Frontend Dev Server: http://localhost:5173 - API Documentation: http://localhost:8000/docs

For more details, see Windows Setup Guide or Quick Start - Windows.

docs.title: Linux/Raspberry Pi Setup
docs.text: Calvin provides automated setup scripts for Raspberry Pi and Linux systems. These scripts handle complete system configuration including user creation, service setup, and display configuration.

docs.title: Production Setup (Raspberry Pi)
docs.text:
For production deployment on Raspberry Pi:

# One-command installation
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

# Or using curl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

What it does: - Creates calvin user if needed - Installs all system dependencies (Python, Node.js, UV, etc.) - Clones the repository to /home/calvin/calvin - Installs backend dependencies (with linux extra for keyboard support) - Installs and builds frontend for production - Configures systemd services for auto-start - Sets up display and kiosk mode - Configures auto-login and X server

After setup: 

sudo reboot

After reboot, the dashboard will automatically start and be available at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Development Setup (Raspberry Pi)
docs.text:
For development with hot-reload on Raspberry Pi:

# Development installation with hot-reload
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo bash

# Or using curl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo bash

What it does: - Everything from production setup, plus: - Creates 4GB swap file (for Pi 3B+ with limited RAM) - Uses venv for backend (more stable on Pi 3B+) - Installs dev dependencies - Configures hot-reload for both backend and frontend - Frontend dev server runs on port 5173

After setup: 

sudo reboot

After reboot: - Backend runs with hot-reload (code changes auto-reload) - Frontend runs with hot-reload (Vite dev server on port 5173) - Dashboard available at http://localhost:5173

docs.title: Using Different Branches
docs.text:
# Production setup with develop branch
export GIT_BRANCH=develop
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo -E bash

# Development setup with develop branch
export GIT_BRANCH=develop
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo -E bash

Note: Use sudo -E to preserve environment variables. Without -E, sudo will not pass GIT_BRANCH or GIT_REPO to the script, and it will default to the main branch.

Important: Export the variable first (export GIT_BRANCH=develop) rather than setting it inline (GIT_BRANCH=develop wget ...), as inline assignments don't propagate through pipes to sudo.

docs.title: Using a Fork or Custom Repository
docs.text:
GIT_REPO=https://github.com/yourusername/calvin.git GIT_BRANCH=your-branch \
  wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

docs.title: Linux Development Setup (Non-Raspberry Pi)
docs.text:
For development on a Linux machine (not Raspberry Pi):

# Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin

# Install dependencies (includes evdev for keyboard support)
make install

# Start development servers
make dev

Or manually:

# Install backend dependencies (includes evdev for keyboard support)
cd backend
uv sync --extra linux --extra dev
cd ../frontend
npm install

# Start development servers (in separate terminals)
# Terminal 1 - Backend:
cd backend
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

# Terminal 2 - Frontend:
cd frontend
npm run dev

Note: The scripts/setup.sh and scripts/setup-dev.sh scripts are for Raspberry Pi deployment (require root, set up systemd services). For Linux development, use the Makefile or manual commands above.

For more details, see Linux Setup Guide or Setup Scripts Documentation.

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Builds

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Polkit (PolicyKit) rules have been added to the installation scripts to allow the calvin user to restart the calvin-backend and calvin-frontend services without requiring sudo or password authentication.

docs.title: Polkit Rule File: 50-calvin-restart.rules
docs.text:
This rule file is automatically created during installation in /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-restart.rules and grants the calvin user permission to manage (start, stop, restart) the Calvin services.

Rule Content: 

polkit.addRule(function(action, subject) {
    if (action.id == "org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units" &&
        subject.user == "calvin") {
        // Allow managing calvin-backend and calvin-frontend services
        var unit = action.lookup("unit");
        if (unit == "calvin-backend.service" || unit == "calvin-frontend.service") {
            return polkit.Result.YES;
        }
    }
});

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The polkit rules are automatically configured during first-boot setup in both: - rpi-image/first-boot/setup.sh (production setup) - rpi-image/first-boot/setup-dev.sh (development setup)

docs.title: Manual Setup (For Existing Installations)
docs.text:
If you have an existing installation that doesn't have these rules, you can add them manually:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/polkit-1/rules.d
sudo tee /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-restart.rules > /dev/null << 'EOF'
polkit.addRule(function(action, subject) {
    if (action.id == "org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units" &&
        subject.user == "calvin") {
        // Allow managing calvin-backend and calvin-frontend services
        var unit = action.lookup("unit");
        if (unit == "calvin-backend.service" || unit == "calvin-frontend.service") {
            return polkit.Result.YES;
        }
    }
});
EOF
sudo chmod 644 /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-restart.rules

After creating the file, the polkit daemon should automatically pick up the new rules. If needed, you can restart polkit:

sudo systemctl restart polkit

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
To verify the rules are working, try restarting a service as the calvin user:

su - calvin
systemctl restart calvin-backend
systemctl restart calvin-frontend

If the rules are working correctly, these commands should succeed without prompting for a password.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• The rules are scoped to only allow management of calvin-backend.service and calvin-frontend.service
  • Only the calvin user is granted these permissions
  • The rules do not grant permission to manage other systemd units or perform other privileged operations

docs.title: Privileged helper scripts (sudo NOPASSWD)
docs.text:
The backend may run /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh (and reboot via /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh) with sudo under a narrow sudoers rule, e.g.:

calvin ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh

Those files must be immutable from the app’s perspective:

  • Owner/group: root:root
  • Mode: 0755 (or stricter; sudo runs them as root, so the app user does not need write access)
  • /usr/local/bin should remain root-owned and not writable by calvin (default on most systems)

If the script were owned by calvin, anyone who could modify code running as calvin could replace the helper and gain root the next time sudo executed that path.

Setup scripts install these helpers with install_privileged_sudo_helper_script in scripts/setup-common.sh (root-owned). Existing systems that still have chown calvin:calvin on those files should fix permissions once:

sudo chown root:root /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh
sudo chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh

New installs use ALL=(root) in sudoers for these helpers; older systems may still have ALL=(ALL) until setup is re-run or /etc/sudoers.d/calvin-* is updated.

docs.title: Related Files
docs.text:
• /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-reboot.rules - Allows calvin user to reboot the system
  • /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-restart.rules - Allows calvin user to restart services

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If service restarts still fail:

  1. Check if the rule file exists: 

    ls -l /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-restart.rules

  2. Check polkit logs: 

    journalctl -u polkit -n 50

  3. Verify the rule syntax: 

    pkaction --version  # Should be 0.106+ for JavaScript rules

  4. Test with pkcheck: 

    pkcheck --action-id org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units --allow-user-interaction

  5. Restart polkit: 

    sudo systemctl restart polkit

docs.text: Pre-commit hooks automatically run linting and formatting checks before each commit, preventing code with errors from being committed.

docs.title: One-time Setup
docs.text:
# From the project root
cd backend
uv run pre-commit install

This will install the hooks into your .git/hooks directory.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
When you run git commit, the hooks will automatically:

  1. Backend (Ruff):
  2. Run ruff check --fix to auto-fix linting issues
  3. Run ruff format to format code

  4. If issues remain that can't be auto-fixed, the commit will be blocked

  5. Frontend (ESLint + Prettier):

  6. Run ESLint with auto-fix
  7. Run Prettier to format code

docs.title: Bypassing Hooks (if needed)
docs.text:
If you need to bypass the hooks for a specific commit (not recommended):

git commit --no-verify -m "your message"

docs.title: Updating Hooks
docs.text:
If the pre-commit configuration changes, update the hooks:

uv run pre-commit install --update-config

docs.title: Running Hooks Manually
docs.text:
You can run the hooks on all files without committing:

# From project root
cd backend
uv run pre-commit run --all-files

docs.title: Hooks not running
docs.text:
• Make sure you ran uv run pre-commit install from the backend directory
  • Check that .git/hooks/pre-commit exists

docs.title: "pre-commit: command not found"
docs.text:
• Use uv run pre-commit instead of just pre-commit
  • Or ensure pre-commit is installed: uv pip install pre-commit

docs.title: Setup Scripts Documentation
docs.text: Calvin provides automated setup scripts for different environments. These scripts have been refactored for better maintainability and robustness.

docs.title: Script Structure
docs.text:
The setup scripts use a shared utility library (scripts/setup-common.sh) that provides common functions for: - Logging and error handling - User management - Package installation - Service configuration - Verification steps

This shared approach reduces code duplication and makes the scripts more maintainable.

docs.title: Production Setup (scripts/setup.sh)
docs.text:
Purpose: Complete production setup for Raspberry Pi or Linux systems.

Features: - Creates calvin user if it doesn't exist - Installs all system dependencies - Installs UV (Python package manager) - Installs Node.js 20+ - Clones/configures Git repository - Installs backend dependencies (production + linux extras) - Installs frontend dependencies (production) - Builds frontend for production - Creates data directories - Configures systemd services - Sets up display and kiosk mode - Configures auto-start on boot

Usage:

# Standard installation (main branch)
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

# Or using curl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

Using a Different Branch:

export GIT_BRANCH=develop
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo -E bash

Note: Use sudo -E to preserve environment variables. Without -E, sudo will not pass GIT_BRANCH or GIT_REPO to the script, and it will default to the main branch.

Important: Export the variable first (export GIT_BRANCH=develop) rather than setting it inline (GIT_BRANCH=develop wget ...), as inline assignments don't propagate through pipes to sudo.

Using a Fork or Custom Repository:

GIT_REPO=https://github.com/yourusername/calvin.git GIT_BRANCH=your-branch \
  wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

What Happens: 1. System packages are updated 2. All dependencies are installed 3. Repository is cloned/updated to /home/calvin/calvin 4. Backend and frontend are built and configured 5. Systemd services are installed and enabled 6. Display is configured for kiosk mode 7. System is ready - reboot required to start services

After Setup: 

sudo reboot

After reboot, the dashboard will automatically start and be available at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Development Setup (scripts/setup-dev.sh)
docs.text:
Purpose: Development setup with hot reload for Raspberry Pi.

Features: - Everything from production setup, plus: - Creates 4GB swap file (for Pi 3B+ with limited RAM) - Uses venv for backend (more stable on Pi 3B+) - Installs dev dependencies - Creates .dev marker file for hot reload - Configures dev-specific frontend service (Vite dev server) - Sets up hot reload for both backend and frontend - Connects to dev server on port 5173

Usage:

# Standard development installation
wget -O- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo bash

# Or using curl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo bash

Using a Different Branch:

export GIT_BRANCH=develop
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/main/scripts/setup-dev.sh | sudo -E bash

Note: Use sudo -E to preserve environment variables. Without -E, sudo will not pass GIT_BRANCH or GIT_REPO to the script, and it will default to the main branch.

Important: Export the variable first (export GIT_BRANCH=develop) rather than setting it inline (GIT_BRANCH=develop curl ...), as inline assignments don't propagate through pipes to sudo.

What Happens: 1. Same as production setup, but with development features 2. Swap file is created for better performance 3. Backend uses venv (more stable than UV on Pi 3B+) 4. Dev dependencies are installed 5. Hot reload is enabled for both backend and frontend 6. Frontend dev server runs on port 5173

After Setup: 

sudo reboot

After reboot: - Backend runs with hot reload (code changes auto-reload) - Frontend runs with hot reload (Vite dev server on port 5173) - Dashboard available at http://localhost:5173

Development Workflow: - Make code changes in /home/calvin/calvin - Backend automatically reloads on file changes - Frontend automatically reloads via Vite HMR - No manual restart needed

docs.title: Windows Development Setup (setup-windows.ps1)
docs.text:
Purpose: Development setup for Windows.

Features: - Checks and installs prerequisites (Python, Node.js, UV) - Handles Git repository (switches to develop branch) - Installs backend dependencies (dev extras) - Installs frontend dependencies - Improved error handling and validation - Better user feedback

Usage:

# Run from project root
.\setup-windows.ps1

What Happens: 1. Checks for Python 3.11+, Node.js 20+, Git 2. Installs UV if not present 3. Switches to develop branch (if Git available) 4. Installs backend dependencies with dev extras 5. Installs frontend dependencies 6. Provides instructions for starting development

After Setup:

Start development servers:

# Terminal 1 - Backend
cd backend
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

# Terminal 2 - Frontend
cd frontend
npm run dev

Note: Keyboard input uses a mock handler on Windows. Full keyboard support is available on Linux/Raspberry Pi.

docs.text:
All scripts support environment variables for customization:

Variable Description Default GIT_REPO Git repository URL https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git GIT_BRANCH Git branch to use main CALVIN_DIR Installation directory /home/calvin/calvin (Linux) CALVIN_USER User to run services calvin (Linux) LOG_FILE Log file path /var/log/calvin-setup.log (Linux)

docs.text: The setup scripts have test suites to ensure they work correctly:

brew install bats-core

# Ubuntu/Debian

docs.title: Script Improvements
docs.text: The scripts have been refactored with the following improvements:

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
• Shared utilities: Common functions in setup-common.sh
  • Modular structure: Clear separation of concerns
  • Consistent error handling: Standardized error messages and exit codes

docs.title: Robustness
docs.text:
• Strict error handling: set -euo pipefail in bash scripts
  • Validation: Checks for prerequisites and verifies installations
  • Logging: Comprehensive logging to track setup progress
  • Verification: Post-setup verification steps

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text:
• Clear progress messages: Color-coded output
  • Error messages: Helpful error messages with suggestions
  • Documentation: Clear instructions and next steps

docs.title: Script Fails During Installation
docs.text:
1. Check logs: 

    # Linux
sudo cat /var/log/calvin-setup.log

# Or check the repository log
cat /home/calvin/calvin/backend/logs/calvin-update.log

  2. Verify prerequisites:

  3. Python 3.11+ installed
  4. Node.js 20+ installed
  5. Git installed

  6. Root/sudo access (for Linux scripts)

  7. Check disk space: 

    df -h

  8. Verify network connectivity: 

    ping github.com
curl -I https://github.com

docs.title: Scripts Not Found When Downloaded
docs.text:
When downloading scripts via wget/curl, the scripts rely on setup-common.sh being in the same directory. The scripts will: 1. Try to find setup-common.sh in the same directory 2. Fall back to current directory 3. Show an error if not found

For repository-based usage (most common), the scripts work correctly as they're all in the scripts/ directory.

docs.title: Services Not Starting
docs.text:
1. Check service status: 

    sudo systemctl status calvin-backend
sudo systemctl status calvin-frontend
# Or for dev mode:
sudo systemctl status calvin-frontend-dev

  2. Check logs: 

    sudo journalctl -u calvin-backend -n 50
sudo journalctl -u calvin-frontend -n 50

  3. Verify permissions: 

    ls -la /home/calvin/calvin
sudo chown -R calvin:calvin /home/calvin/calvin

docs.title: Development Mode Issues
docs.text:
1. Hot reload not working:
  2. Verify .dev file exists: ls -la /home/calvin/calvin/backend/.dev
  3. Check backend service logs for --reload flag

  4. Verify frontend dev service is running

  5. Swap file issues:

  6. Check swap: free -h
  7. Verify swap file: ls -lh /swapfile
  8. If needed, recreate: sudo swapoff /swapfile && sudo rm /swapfile

docs.title: Updating After Setup
docs.text:
After initial setup, use the update script:

update-calvin.sh

Or with force flag to rebuild dependencies: 

update-calvin.sh --force

docs.title: Test Repository Setup for E2E Tests
docs.text: This document explains how to set up a test GitHub repository for end-to-end testing of the plugin installation system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The E2E tests (test_github_plugin_e2e.py) use a real GitHub repository to validate the full plugin installation flow. This provides confidence that the system works with real-world GitHub repositories.

docs.title: Option 1: Use an Existing Test Repository
docs.text:
If a test repository already exists, set the environment variable:

export TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins"
export TEST_GITHUB_BRANCH="main"  # Optional, defaults to "main"

docs.title: Option 2: Create Your Own Test Repository
docs.text:
1. Create a new GitHub repository (public or private with appropriate access)

  2. Repository structure: 

    test-plugins/
├── plugins.json          # Optional: manifest file
├── plugin1/
│   ├── plugin.json
│   └── plugin.py
├── plugin2/
│   ├── plugin.json
│   ├── plugin.py
│   └── frontend/
│       └── Component.vue
└── README.md

  3. Example plugin.json: 

    {
  "id": "test_e2e_plugin",
  "name": "Test E2E Plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "service",
  "description": "A test plugin for E2E testing",
  "author": "Test Author",
  "license": "MIT"
}

  4. Example plugin.py: 

    """Test plugin for E2E testing."""
from typing import Any
from app.plugins.base import PluginType
from app.plugins.hooks import hookimpl

@hookimpl
def register_plugin_types() -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Register plugin type."""
    return [{
        "type_id": "test_e2e_plugin",
        "plugin_type": PluginType.SERVICE
    }]

  5. Optional: plugins.json manifest: 

    {
  "plugins": [
    {
      "id": "test_e2e_plugin",
      "name": "Test E2E Plugin",
      "path": "plugin1",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "type": "service",
      "description": "A test plugin for E2E testing"
    }
  ]
}

  6. Push to GitHub: 

    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: Test plugins for E2E testing"
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins.git
git push -u origin main

docs.title: Run all E2E tests:
docs.text:
cd backend
uv run pytest tests/e2e/test_github_plugin_e2e.py -m e2e -v

docs.title: Run with custom repository:
docs.text:
TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins" \
uv run pytest tests/e2e/test_github_plugin_e2e.py -m e2e -v

docs.title: Skip E2E tests (default in CI):
docs.text:
# E2E tests are marked with @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow
# They won't run unless explicitly requested
uv run pytest  # Skips E2E tests

docs.title: Test Behavior
docs.text:
• Network check: Tests skip if network is unavailable
  • Repository check: Tests skip if repository doesn't exist or is inaccessible
  • Graceful degradation: Tests provide helpful skip messages
  • Cleanup: Tests clean up installed plugins after running

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
E2E tests are marked with @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow, so they:

  • Skip by default in CI/CD pipelines (fast, reliable builds)
  • Can be run manually for validation
  • Can be run in scheduled jobs (e.g., nightly builds)

docs.title: Example CI configuration:
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run unit and integration tests
        run: uv run pytest -m "not e2e"  # Skip E2E tests

  test-e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'  # Run on schedule only
    steps:
      - name: Run E2E tests
        run: |
          export TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/calvin-dashboard/test-plugins"
          uv run pytest tests/e2e/ -m e2e -v

docs.title: Benefits of E2E Tests
docs.text:
1. Real-world validation: Tests actual GitHub API integration
  2. Catch integration issues: Network problems, rate limits, API changes
  3. Validate branch fallback: Real main/master branch behavior
  4. Test actual plugin structure: Real plugin.json and plugin.py files

docs.title: Mocked Tests (Default)
docs.text:
• ✅ Fast (no network calls)
  • ✅ Reliable (no external dependencies)
  • ✅ Test error cases easily
  • ✅ Run in CI/CD without network

docs.title: E2E Tests (Optional)
docs.text:
• ✅ Real-world validation
  • ✅ Catch integration issues
  • ❌ Slower (network calls)
  • ❌ Can be flaky (network issues)
  • ❌ Require internet connection

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
• Use mocked tests for regular CI/CD (fast, reliable)
  • Use E2E tests for:
  • Manual validation before releases
  • Scheduled nightly builds
  • Local development validation
  • Debugging integration issues

docs.title: Mocked Tests (Default)
docs.text:
GitHub API: - Uses unittest.mock.patch to mock httpx.AsyncClient.get - Returns mock zip file content - Tests branch fallback by returning 404 then 200 - Fast, reliable, no network dependencies

System Commands: - Uses unittest.mock.patch to mock subprocess.run - Tests both success and failure scenarios - Tests fallback from systemctl to dbus

docs.title: E2E Tests (Optional)
docs.text: Real GitHub Repository: - Uses actual httpx.AsyncClient to call GitHub API - Tests with real repository structure - Validates actual branch fallback behavior - Gracefully skips if network/repo unavailable - Can be configured via TEST_GITHUB_REPO environment variable

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All tests use temporary directories for isolation
  • Tests clean up after themselves
  • Integration tests use mocked external services
  • Unit tests focus on business logic
  • Integration tests focus on API contracts
